question: Inhibin: a new circulating marker of hydatidiform mole?
answer: Serum inhibin was significantly higher in patients with complete hydatidiform mole before evacuation (median 8.3 U/ml) than in normal women at the same stage of pregnancy (2.8 U/ml), and it fell significantly after evacuation to follicular-phase levels (0.4 U/ml). This supports inhibin as a circulating marker of hydatidiform mole. Molar tissue also contained high concentrations of inhibin (cytosol median 578 U/ml). None of the four patients whose post-evacuation serum inhibin was 0.4 U/ml or less developed persistent trophoblastic disease. In a second study of patients with hydatidiform mole, invasive mole or choriocarcinoma, serum inhibin A was elevated in 10/17 patients and inhibin B in 4/17, whereas HCG and HCGbeta were high in all. In patients followed during chemotherapy, inhibin A correlated with HCG and HCGbeta and normalized faster than HCG in some patients, while inhibin B did not correlate with HCGbeta.

question: Discharging patients earlier from Winnipeg hospitals: does it adversely affect quality of care?
answer: In Winnipeg's seven large acute care hospitals, length of stay fell significantly (11.1% to 22.0%) over 1989-90 to 1992-93 for AMI, bronchitis/asthma, TURP and uterine/adnexal procedures without a consistent rise in 30-day readmission rates, so earlier discharge did not appear to adversely affect quality of care. The only significant readmission change was a rise for uterine or adnexal procedures between the first and second year, after which it stayed constant; physician visits after discharge changed little (a slight rise for AMI in year one, a slight fall for bronchitis/asthma). Across the Winnipeg hospitals in 1992-93, there was no significant correlation between length of stay and readmission rates in any of the four categories, nor between length of stay and physician visits for AMI and bronchitis/asthma.

The only significant readmission change was a rise for uterine or adnexal procedures between the first and second year, after which it stayed constant; physician visits after discharge changed little (a slight rise for AMI in year one, a slight fall for bronchitis/asthma).

Across the Winnipeg hospitals in 1992-93, there was no significant correlation between length of stay and readmission rates in any of the four categories, nor between length of stay and physician visits for AMI and bronchitis/asthma.

limitations.text: The Winnipeg study was a retrospective descriptive analysis limited to four diagnostic categories and to 30-day readmissions and physician visits; it did not assess mortality, patient-reported outcomes, or other quality measures.
Exclusions (in-hospital deaths, stays over 60 days, transfers, out-of-province patients) and the descriptive design mean that trends and hospital-level correlations cannot establish causation.

question: Vertical lines in distal esophageal mucosa (VLEM): a true endoscopic manifestation of esophagitis in children?
answer: In a retrospective review of pediatric esophageal biopsies, VLEM as the only endoscopic abnormality was associated with histologic esophagitis: only 1 of 41 biopsies (2.4%) in the VLEM group was histologically normal, versus 57.5% of biopsies from endoscopically normal mucosa. Most children with VLEM had eosinophilic esophagitis (34 of 41, 83%), and it was usually of moderate to severe intensity (31 of 34, 91.2%). VLEM was fairly specific but not very sensitive for eosinophilic esophagitis (specificity 0.85, sensitivity 0.5), and for moderate to severe eosinophilic esophagitis (specificity 0.88, sensitivity 0.73), so its absence does not exclude disease.

question: Are head and neck specific quality of life measures necessary?
answer: Head and neck-specific health status domains appear distinct from those captured by a general QOL measure: in 55 head and neck cancer patients, the Head&Neck Survey correlated more strongly with other head and neck-specific measures than with the general health measure. Eating/swallowing and speech/communication domains were not well correlated with general health domains, and appearance was not fully reflected by any other domain, so general measures may miss these concerns. Not every head and neck domain was distinct: head and neck pain was highly correlated with general bodily pain (r=0.88), which suggests overlap between these pain domains and that general measures may partly capture pain.

question: Does the SCL 90-R obsessive-compulsive dimension identify cognitive impairments?
answer: In 19 adults with malignant brain tumors, the SCL 90-R Obsessive-Compulsive subscale was not related to objective measures of attention or verbal memory, so it did not identify objectively measured cognitive impairment. The subscale was instead strongly related to depression (r = .81), anxiety (r = .66), and subjective memory complaints (r = .75). Depression accounted for 66% of the variance in subscale scores, with anxiety adding 6%.

question: Hypotension in patients with coronary disease: can profound hypotensive events cause myocardial ischaemic events?
answer: In patients with ischaemic heart disease on anti-anginal/hypotensive drugs, ST-segment ischaemic events were significantly associated with preceding ambulatory hypotensive events (chi2 = 40.2, p<0.0001), and 14 hypotension-induced ischaemic events occurred in 8 of 25 patients. Most hypotension-induced ischaemic events (13 of 14) were preceded by a fall in diastolic pressure (median 57.5 mm Hg), while six were preceded by a fall in systolic pressure. Patients who had hypotension-induced ischaemic events were more often on multiple hypotensive drug regimens (8/8 vs 9/17, p = 0.022).

question: Fatigue in primary Sjögren's syndrome: is there a link with the fibromyalgia syndrome?
answer: Fatigue was common in primary Sjögren's syndrome (50/74, 68%), but fibromyalgia was present in only 9/74 (12%) of pSS patients. So at most 9 of the 50 fatigued patients could have fibromyalgia, and most fatigue occurred without it. Fatigue was significantly more prevalent in pSS than in the lupus control group (68% vs 50%, p<0.0087). Fibromyalgia was also numerically more frequent in pSS than in lupus (12% vs 5%), and was absent in the lupus patients with secondary Sjögren's syndrome, although fatigue was present in 54% of them. The authors noted that the fibromyalgia prevalence they found did not correspond with previously reported figures for pSS.

question: Is alexithymia a risk factor for unexplained physical symptoms in general medical outpatients?
answer: In a cross-sectional study of 321 internal medicine outpatients, those with medically unexplained physical symptoms (169 patients) were overall not more alexithymic than those with explained symptoms, so alexithymia was not shown to be a risk factor. Among patients with unexplained symptoms, alexithymia was not associated with subjective health experience or use of medical services. Higher alexithymia was seen only in a subgroup: patients with unexplained symptoms and a mental disorder who also denied any connection between emotional problems and their physical symptoms.

question: Is semi-closed endarterectomy of the superficial femoral artery combined with a short venous bypass in case of insufficient venous material an acceptable alternative for limb-threatening ischemia?
answer: In 30 patients with critical leg ischemia and insufficient vein, semiclosed SFA endarterectomy combined with a short venous bypass gave cumulative primary patency of 60.3% at 1 year and 48.4% at 3 years, with limb salvage of 68.6% at both 1 and 3 years.

question: Antral follicle assessment as a tool for predicting outcome in IVF--is it a better predictor than age and FSH?
answer: In a prospective study of 224 IVF patients, baseline antral follicle count >6 was associated with a much higher clinical pregnancy rate than count ≤6 (51% vs 19%), and this difference remained significant after controlling for maternal age and basal FSH. Cycle cancellation was also far more frequent with antral follicles ≤6 than >6 (33% vs 1%), although cancellation also rose with advancing age and elevated basal FSH. In a separate cohort of women who conceived after IVF/ICSI, AFC was the only ovarian reserve marker (compared with FSH, basal oestradiol and oestradiol response) that differed between miscarriage and ongoing pregnancy groups, though its discriminative ability for miscarriage was low (AUC 0.588).

question: Acute respiratory distress syndrome in children with malignancy--can we predict outcome?
answer: In a retrospective review of 17 children with malignancy and ARDS on mechanical ventilation, 6 (35.3%) survived, and ventilator parameters (peak inspiratory pressure, PEEP, ventilation index) distinguished survivors from non-survivors by day 3. Oxygenation efficiency measures (PaO2/FIO2 and P(A-a)O2) were significantly related to outcome from day 8 after the start of mechanical ventilation, so outcome prediction from respiratory data became possible early (day 3) and strengthened later.

question: Does tranexamic acid reduce desmopressin-induced hyperfibrinolysis?
answer: In a randomized trial of 100 CABG patients, adding tranexamic acid to desmopressin reduced fibrinolysis markers versus desmopressin alone: fibrin split products were lower (13.5 vs 21.2 ng/mL, P=.0001) and postoperative fibrinogen was higher (167 vs 113 mg/dL, P=.0001). The combination also improved clinical hemostasis: chest drainage was lower (623 vs 1010 mL), and fewer patients needed donor blood or products (24% vs 74%). Postoperative hemoglobin was higher (9.1 vs 7.6 g/dL).

question: Is specialty care associated with improved survival of patients with congestive heart failure?
answer: In a large retrospective VHA cohort of CHF patients, those receiving mixed general medicine and cardiology outpatient care had the lowest 1-year mortality (19% unadjusted), and general-medicine-only care carried a higher adjusted risk of death (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.15-1.38) than mixed care. Patients with no general medicine or cardiology follow-up had the worst outcomes (29% unadjusted mortality; adjusted RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.28-1.72 vs. mixed care), and the GM-only versus mixed difference was replicated in a second cohort (RR 1.25, 1.14-1.37). Cardiology-only care was not significantly different from mixed care (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.94-1.34), so the survival benefit appears tied to cardiology involvement (alone or combined with general medicine) rather than to either alone being clearly superior.

question: Locoregional opening of the rodent blood-brain barrier for paclitaxel using Nd:YAG laser-induced thermo therapy: a new concept of adjuvant glioma therapy?
answer: In rats, Nd:YAG laser-induced thermotherapy (LITT) of the forebrain opened the blood-brain barrier locally, shown by extravasation of Evans blue, C3C, fibrinogen and IgM, and HPLC confirmed that paclitaxel crossed the disrupted barrier. The authors framed this locoregional BBB disruption as a possible way to deliver chemotherapeutic agents into brain tissue to treat malignant glioma.

question: Can progression of valvar aortic stenosis be predicted accurately?
answer: In a cohort of 169 men and 88 women with aortic stenosis, progression was found to be exponentially related to valvar calcification grade and to the initial hemodynamic severity (transaortic gradient), and was judged sufficiently predictable for clinical purposes. The same cohort showed that progression rate depends on calcification degree (0 to III) and is exponentially correlated with initial aortic valve opening area. Specific area thresholds by calcification grade (e.g., AVA below 0.75 cm2 with no calcification, or 1.0 cm2 with grade III) identify patients likely to need surgery in the following years. Neither age, sex, nor etiology of the valvar obstruction significantly influenced the progression of aortic stenosis.

question: Sub-classification of low-grade cerebellar astrocytoma: is it clinically meaningful?
answer: In a Danish cohort of children with cerebellar astrocytoma, histological sub-classification did not predict survival: pilocytic and fibrillary astrocytoma showed no survival difference, and the Kernohan and WHO systems had no predictive value. The Daumas-Duport grading system was judged unsuitable as a prognostic tool for low-grade posterior fossa astrocytomas. The factors that did predict survival were clinical or surgical rather than histological: gross-total surgical removal and tumour location in the cerebellum proper rather than the fourth ventricle. Overall survival was 81% at 15-40 years of follow-up.

question: Is eligibility for a chemotherapy protocol a good prognostic factor for invasive bladder cancer after radical cystectomy?
answer: Patients eligible for and entered into an adjuvant chemotherapy protocol (SAKK 09/84) after radical cystectomy had better outcomes than matched and remaining non-protocol patients: median overall survival was 76.3 months vs 52.1 months (matched) and 20.3 months (remaining). Median recurrence-free survival was also longer in the protocol group (67.2 months) than in the matched (16.0 months) and remaining groups (9.4 months). Tumor progression occurred in 46% of the protocol group vs 69% of the matched and 65% of the remaining groups (P<.05), and cancer-related death was 40% vs 57% and 56%, respectively. This happened even though the trial itself had a negative result, suggesting that eligibility itself is associated with a favorable prognosis rather than the chemotherapy effect.

question: Is gastric electrical stimulation superior to standard pharmacologic therapy in improving GI symptoms, healthcare resources, and long-term health care benefits?
answer: In a small comparison of gastroparesis patients, gastric electrical stimulation (GES) produced more sustained symptom improvement over 36 months than intensive medical therapy. Healthcare resource use (IDIOMS score) improved at 12, 24 and 36 months with GES, whereas patients on medical therapy deteriorated. GES was also superior in reducing costs at 24 and 36 months. Three of nine patients in the medical therapy group died, mainly from i.v. access-related problems, while none of the GES patients died. Hospital days fell significantly within both groups, with no significant difference between them.

question: Are physicians aware of the side effects of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors?
answer: Physicians showed poor awareness of ACE-inhibitor side effects: in a questionnaire survey, the percentage of correct answers was only 31.9% for cardiologists, 40% for GPs and 33% for allergists. question: Can bedside assessment reliably exclude aspiration following acute stroke?
answer: In a prospective study of 94 acute stroke patients compared with videofluoroscopy, bedside assessment by a speech and language therapist had only 47% sensitivity (NPV 85%), and aspiration went undetected at the bedside in 10 of 20 aspirating patients, so it could not reliably exclude aspiration. The best combination of bedside features (weak voluntary cough plus any alteration in conscious level) reached 75% sensitivity, 72% specificity and 91% NPV, which is still not sufficient to reliably rule out aspiration. Another prospective study found that bedside dysphagia assessment was associated with outcomes such as chest infection, mortality and length of stay, and that videofluoroscopy did not add value to bedside assessment for detecting aspiration. This suggests bedside assessment has prognostic value, though it does not show that it excludes aspiration.

question: Is fetal gender associated with emergency department visits for asthma during pregnancy?
answer: Fetal gender was not associated with having an emergency department visit for asthma during pregnancy (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.85-1.19) in a linked administrative database study of 109,173 live singleton deliveries, 530 of which involved an asthma ED visit. Among women who had an asthma ED visit during pregnancy, fetal gender was also not a significant predictor of adverse pregnancy outcomes (low birth weight, preterm delivery, Caesarian section). ED visits for asthma during pregnancy were instead positively associated with teenage pregnancy, low income, and pregnancy-induced hypertension.

question: Do French lay people and health professionals find it acceptable to breach confidentiality to protect a patient's wife from a sexually transmitted disease?
answer: Acceptability of breaching confidentiality to protect a patient's wife from his STD differed by group. Lay people (mean 11.76) and psychologists (9.28) favoured it far more than physicians (2.90) on a 0-22 scale. Acceptability depended on circumstances. The patient's stated intentions to protect his wife and to inform her about the disease had the greatest impact on ratings. Lay participants were split. Most (n=87) said it depended on the circumstances, 30 wanted an expert consulted, 14 found breaching always acceptable, and 13 found it never acceptable.

question: Chemotherapy and survival in advanced non-small cell lung carcinoma: is pneumologists' skepticism justified?
answer: In a study of 190 patients with advanced NSCLC (stage IV or IIIB) treated in routine care, cytostatic treatment was associated with longer survival in multivariable analysis (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.25-2.76, P=.002), which does not support the skepticism about chemotherapy in this setting. In patients with ECOG performance status 2, median survival was numerically longer with cytostatic treatment than with symptomatic treatment (15 vs 11 weeks), although no statistical test is reported for this subgroup. Absence of weight loss and good performance status (ECOG 0-1) were also significant prognostic factors for survival, and treatment remained a significant prognostic factor in patients with ECOG 0-1.

question: Can folic acid protect against congenital heart defects in Down syndrome?
answer: In a case-control analysis of liveborn children with Down syndrome, first-trimester folic acid use showed no protective effect against heart anomalies overall (adjusted OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.61-1.47). No protective effect was found for specific heart defect subtypes either, including conotruncal defects, ventricular septal defects, ostium secundum atrial septal defects, or endocardial cushion defects. Folic acid exposure was similar between Down syndrome children with heart anomalies (110 of 223, 49%) and those without (84 of 184, 46%).

question: Is breast cancer prognosis inherited?
answer: A Swedish population-based cohort study found that breast cancer prognosis aggregates in families: daughters and sisters of a proband with poor prognosis had a 60% higher 5-year breast cancer mortality than those of a proband with good prognosis (HR 1.6; 95% CI 1.2 to 2.2). Five-year survival was lower among daughters whose mothers died within 5 years (87% vs 91%) and among sisters whose proband sister died within 5 years (70% vs 88%). The association was slightly stronger among sisters (HR 1.8; 95% CI 1.0 to 3.4) than among mother-daughter pairs (HR 1.6; 95% CI 1.1 to 2.3).

question: Is laparoscopic adrenalectomy safe and effective for adrenal masses larger than 7 cm?
answer: In a retrospective series of 18 laparoscopic adrenalectomies for lesions larger than 7 cm (mean 8.3 cm), the procedure was feasible, with a mean operative time of 137 min and mean blood loss of 182 mL. However, the intraoperative complication rate was 16% and 3 cases were converted to open surgery, so safety and effectiveness are only partly supported. In a separate series of laparoscopic adrenalectomies, pheochromocytomas, which were significantly larger than other tumors, required more operating time and longer hospital stays and accounted for 87% of intraoperative and 67% of postoperative complications. No local recurrence was reported after laparoscopic adrenalectomy.

question: Adults with mild intellectual disabilities: can their reading comprehension ability be improved?
answer: In a study of 38 adults with mild intellectual disability, a 15-week text comprehension strategy programme (summarizing, questioning, clarifying, predicting) produced substantial gains on the strategy tests, except for questioning, and an even larger transfer effect to general text comprehension. question: Body diffusion-weighted MR imaging of uterine endometrial cancer: is it helpful in the detection of cancer in nonenhanced MR imaging?
answer: Adding diffusion-weighted (DW) images and fused DW/T2-weighted images to T2-weighted imaging raised detection sensitivity for endometrial cancer from 83% (19/23) to 96% (22/23), so DWI added incremental value to nonenhanced MRI. DWI identified cancer in 3 of the 4 patients whose tumors were missed on T2-weighted images alone; two of those 4 had coexisting leiomyoma. The mean ADC of endometrial cancer ((0.97±0.19)×10^-3 mm²/s) was significantly lower than that of normal endometrium, myometrium, leiomyoma and adenomyosis (p<0.05), which supports the quantitative contrast that makes tumors detectable on DWI.

question: Is there a role for endothelin-1 in the hemodynamic changes during hemodialysis?
answer: In a study of 45 ESRD patients on hemodialysis, intradialytic ET-1 changes tracked hemodynamic status: ET-1 fell significantly in patients with dialysis-induced hypotension (11.75 to 8.56 pg/ml), rose in those with rebound hypertension (11.93 to 16.39 pg/ml), and was unchanged in those with stable hemodynamics. question: Does somatostatin confer insulinostatic effects of neuromedin u in the rat pancreas?
answer: Somatostatin appears to mediate, at least in part, the insulinostatic effect of neuromedin U in the rat pancreas: NmU reduced insulin secretion from perfused rat pancreas, stimulated somatostatin secretion from isolated islets, and blocking somatostatin receptors with cyclosomatostatin reduced NmU-induced inhibition of insulin secretion. NmU stimulated somatostatin secretion at both physiological and supraphysiological glucose concentrations, and the NmU receptor subtype NmUR1 (but not NmUR2) was expressed in the endocrine pancreas, predominantly in the periphery of the islets. Cyclosomatostatin alone increased insulin secretion, consistent with a paracrine inhibitory role of somatostatin within islets.

question: Treadmill training post stroke: are there any secondary benefits?
answer: In a small matched-pair study of chronic stroke survivors, 12 treadmill sessions were followed by significant within-group improvements in depression, mobility and social participation, but there was no significant difference between the treadmill and control groups on any measure. question: Can magnetic resonance imaging accurately predict concordant pain provocation during provocative disc injection?
answer: A combined MR finding of disc protrusion with a high intensity zone (HIZ) correlated significantly with concordant pain provocation on discography (P<0.01), with sensitivity 45.5%, specificity 97.8% and PPV 87.0%. Individual MR findings were not helpful for identifying a disc with concordant pain: disc degeneration (sensitivity 95.4%, specificity 38.8%, PPV 33.9%), disc protrusion (68.2%, 80.6%, 53.6%) and HIZ alone (56.8%, 83.6%, 53.2%). A normal or bulging disc with an HIZ was not associated with reproduction of pain.

question: Standardizing care in medical oncology: are Web-based systems the answer?
answer: In an interview and observation study at 6 Australian hospitals, a Web-based protocol system played a major role in guiding oncology treatment across participating sites. Its use varied by hospital location, clinician role, and experience, so it is not a uniform route to standardized care. The level of education clinicians received about the system was found to be integral to its ongoing use.

question: Is it necessary to insert a nasobiliary drainage tube routinely after endoscopic clearance of the common bile duct in patients with choledocholithiasis-induced cholangitis?
answer: Routine ENBD insertion after endoscopic clearance of CBD stones in choledocholithiasis-induced acute cholangitis does not appear necessary: in a randomized study of 104 patients, cholangitis recurrence at 24 weeks (3.9% vs 3.8%) and hospital stay (7.9 vs 7.9 days) did not differ between ENBD and no-ENBD groups. question: Diagnostic and therapeutic ureteroscopy: is dilatation of ureteral meatus always necessary?
answer: Meatal dilatation is not always necessary: in a retrospective comparison of 286 semirigid ureteroscopies, procedures done without ureteral meatus dilatation (95) had no statistically significant difference in peroperative or postoperative complications compared with those done with dilatation (191), with an overall success rate of 86.5%. question: Are patients willing participants in the new wave of community-based medical education in regional and rural Australia?
answer: In a survey of patients attending rural and regional general practices in New South Wales teaching sessions, 118 of 122 patients consented to medical student involvement in their consultation, and patients were overwhelmingly positive about their doctor and practice being involved in student teaching. Patients felt they played an important role in student teaching. Although they were initially reluctant before the consultation to let students conduct some or all aspects independently, after the consultation they reported they would have accepted higher levels of student involvement than actually occurred. A survey of 625 patients across five specialty teaching clinics found that patients in all specialties shared similar comfort levels and attitudes regarding medical student involvement for the majority of parameters assessed.

question: Does perspective-taking increase patient satisfaction in medical encounters?
answer: In three randomized studies of student-clinicians (N = 608), a perspective-taking instruction produced higher standardized patient satisfaction than a neutral instruction, with small effects (standardized effect sizes 0.13 to 0.31). question: Are adult body circumferences associated with height?
answer: In NHANES III adults, waist and hip circumferences scaled significantly with height after adjustment for age and race (WC power 0.76 in men, 0.80 in women; HC power 0.45 in men, 0.53 in women; all P<0.001), with increments of about 0.2 to 0.5 cm per cm of height. Unadjusted univariate circumference-height models were weak or nonsignificant, so the association emerged mainly after adjusting for age and race. Health status-adjusted models gave similar results. WC/height and HC/height ratios scaled negatively to height in both sexes, and WC/HC scaled negatively to height in women only. In a Glasgow cohort, individuals in the most deprived neighbourhood were shorter and had larger waist circumferences and waist-hip ratios, and a Manchester study found that greater waist girth and lower height were independently related to plasma glucose. These findings are consistent with an inverse height-waist relationship but do not directly test it.

question: Does minimal access major surgery in the newborn hurt less?
answer: In a retrospective matched cohort of neonates undergoing esophageal atresia or congenital diaphragmatic hernia repair, thoracoscopic minimal access surgery did not reduce opioid consumption compared with conventional surgery at 12 h, 24 h, 48 h or 7 days. question: Can dobutamine stress echocardiography induce cardiac troponin elevation?
answer: In a prospective study of 55 analyzable patients referred for dobutamine stress echocardiography, none had elevated cardiac troponin I 18-24 hours after the test, even though about half had inducible ischemia (22% mild, 23.6% moderate, 9% severe). question: Are patients with serious mental illness more likely to be admitted to nursing homes with more deficiencies in care?
answer: In a national cohort of over 1.3 million new nursing home admissions in 2007, patients with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder tended to enter nursing homes with more total and healthcare-related deficiency citations than other patients. Patients with schizophrenia entered facilities averaging 13.3 total and 8.6 healthcare-related deficiencies versus 11.2 and 7.2 for other patients; for bipolar disorder the figures were 12.5 and 8.2 versus 11.2 and 7.2 (all P<0.001). question: Is endometrial polyp formation associated with increased expression of vascular endothelial growth factor and transforming growth factor-beta1?
answer: In a prospective study of 70 premenopausal women, endometrial polyps showed higher VEGF and TGF-β1 expression than adjacent endometrium, with VEGF raised in glandular cells in both cycle phases and TGF-β1 raised in stromal cells in both phases. VEGF in stromal cells was higher in polyps only in the proliferative phase (P=0.006), and TGF-β1 in glandular cells was higher only in the proliferative phase (P=0.02), so the increase depends on cell type and cycle phase. Expression of VEGF and TGF-β1 correlated significantly with steroid receptor (estrogen and progesterone receptor) expression, suggesting a possible link to hormonal regulation.

question: MiraLAX vs. Golytely: is there a significant difference in the adenoma detection rate?
answer: In a post hoc analysis of an RCT of average-risk screening colonoscopy, Golytely was independently associated with higher adenoma detection than MiraLAX on multivariate analysis (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.05-4.98, P=0.04). question: Does a colonoscopy after acute diverticulitis affect its management?
answer: In a retrospective review of 220 patients hospitalized for acute diverticulitis, early (4 to 6 week) post-discharge colonoscopy in 100 patients detected no colonic malignancy and produced no new or different diagnosis, suggesting it did not change management. question: Does route of delivery affect maternal and perinatal outcome in women with eclampsia?
answer: In a randomized trial of 200 eclampsia cases at ≥34 weeks, route of delivery (cesarean vs vaginal) did not significantly change composite maternal outcomes (10.89% vs 7.07%; RR 1.54, 95% CI 0.62-3.81). question: Can early second-look tympanoplasty reduce the rate of conversion to modified radical mastoidectomy?

question: Contrast-enhanced MR imaging of hand and finger joints in patients with early rheumatoid arthritis: do we really need a full dose of gadobenate dimeglumine for assessing synovial enhancement at 3 T?
answer: In 57 patients with early RA imaged at 3 T, half-dose (0.05 mmol/kg) and full-dose (0.1 mmol/kg) gadobenate dimeglumine images showed no difference in RAMRIS, tenosynovitis scores, image quality, or assessment of synovial enhancement (P = 1). Quantitatively, synovial signal intensity was significantly lower at half dose than at full dose (mean 914.35 vs 1022, P<.001), but the half-dose and full-dose ratios were highly correlated (r = 0.875). Because of this correlation, a regression formula can convert normalized half-dose synovial enhancement ratios to full-dose values.

question: Globulomaxillary cysts--do they really exist?
answer: The globulomaxillary cyst is no longer regarded as its own entity; in a retrospective series of 17 cases first diagnosed as globulomaxillary cysts, all were reassigned to other recognized entities. The reassigned lesions were 7 lateral periodontal cysts, 4 radicular cysts, 2 keratocystic odontogenic tumours, 1 adenomatoid odontogenic tumour, 1 periapical granuloma, 1 residual cyst and 1 undefined jaw cyst. Cystic lesions resembling the former globulomaxillary cyst image still occur in practice, but they belong to other pathological entities, not to a distinct fissural cyst type.

question: Telemedicine and type 1 diabetes: is technology per se sufficient to improve glycaemic control?
answer: In a 6-month study of smartphone insulin dose advisor users, adding telemonitoring/teleconsultation did not improve HbA1c further among high users (-0.49% with vs -0.52% without; P=0.879), so the telemedicine function added no measurable benefit in that group. Among low users of the insulin dose advisor, those who also received teleconsultation support tended to improve HbA1c more than those without (-0.93% vs -0.46%; P=0.084), suggesting human support may help when engagement with the technology is low, although this was not statistically significant. Engagement with the technology differed between groups: the proportion of meals using the advisor stayed stable in high users (P=0.107) but fell significantly in low users over 6 months (P=0.005).

question: Does sex influence the response to intravenous thrombolysis in ischemic stroke?
answer: In a large registry of 45,079 alteplase-treated patients, adjusted functional independence at 3 months did not differ between sexes (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97-1.09), so sex did not meaningfully influence functional response to thrombolysis. In the same registry, male sex was associated with higher adjusted risks of mortality (OR 1.19) and symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (OR 1.25), although unadjusted analysis showed higher mortality in women and better functional independence in men. In 369 rt-PA-treated patients monitored with transcranial Doppler, men and women did not differ in recanalization rates (complete 34.2% vs 31.2%; p=0.6), time to recanalization, or 3-month clinical outcome after adjustment.

question: Clinical identifiers for early-stage primary/idiopathic adhesive capsulitis: are we seeing the real picture?
answer: In a cross-sectional study of 64 patients clinically diagnosed with early-stage adhesive capsulitis, only 16 (25%) showed a positive anesthetic response (≥70% pain relief in passive external rotation after intra-articular local anesthetic), the reference standard used to test 8 Delphi-derived clinical identifiers. Global loss of passive range of movement (OR=0.26), pain at end of range of all measured active movements (OR=0.06), and global loss of passive glenohumeral movements (OR=0.23) were associated with a positive anesthetic response in univariate analysis, with odds ratios below 1 indicating reduced odds. After stepwise removal of variables, only pain at the end of range of all measured active movements remained, and it was associated with reduced odds of a positive anesthetic response, so none of the proposed identifiers was supported as a positive predictor.

question: Does the sex of acute stroke patients influence the effectiveness of rt-PA?
answer: In 369 rt-PA-treated stroke patients with acute TCD monitoring, men and women did not differ in complete recanalization (34.2% vs 31.2%), partial recanalization, no recanalization (p=0.6), time to recanalization, or 3-month clinical outcome after multiple regression adjustment. In a large register of 45,079 alteplase-treated patients, men had higher unadjusted functional independence at 3 months and women had higher unadjusted mortality, but after adjusting for confounders there was no sex difference in functional outcome (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97-1.09). After adjustment in the same register, male sex was associated with higher mortality (OR 1.19) and higher symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage risk (OR 1.25), though the rate of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage did not differ in the unadjusted comparison (P=0.13).

question: HIF1A as a major vascular endothelial growth factor regulator: do its polymorphisms have an association with age-related macular degeneration?
answer: In a study of 87 AMD patients and 80 controls, the HIF1A polymorphisms rs11549465 and rs11549467 showed no statistically significant difference in distribution between AMD patients and healthy subjects. In the same study, the CFH polymorphism rs1061170 was associated with AMD: carrying at least one C allele increased risk independent of age (OR 2.42, 95% CI 1.22-4.81), and the ancestral T allele was protective (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.34-0.83). SKIV2L and MYRIP polymorphisms showed no significant association.

question: May student examiners be reasonable substitute examiners for faculty in an undergraduate OSCE on medical emergencies?
answer: In a randomized OSCE on emergency medicine management (207 third-year students; 110 with student examiners, 98 with faculty examiners), students in the student-examiner track scored significantly higher on the Trauma-Management, Airway-Management and Obstetrical-Emergencies stations and on overall OSCE score, while the Pediatric-Emergencies station score was significantly higher in the faculty-examiner track; effect sizes were mostly small. question: Does radiotherapy of the primary rectal cancer affect prognosis after pelvic exenteration for recurrent rectal cancer?
answer: In a retrospective review of 87 patients undergoing pelvic exenteration for locally recurrent rectal cancer, prior radiotherapy for the primary tumour was associated with worse outcomes, including lower disease-free survival (p = 0.022). Patients previously irradiated for the primary cancer needed more radical exenterations (68% vs 44%), had lower rates of clear resection margins (63% vs 87%), and had more surgical complications per patient. Even among patients with clear margins, overall survival and disease-free survival were lower in those with prior primary radiotherapy, and the survival difference persisted in multivariate analysis correcting for T and N stage of the primary tumour.

question: Rectal cancer threatening or affecting the prostatic plane: is partial prostatectomy oncologically adequate?
answer: In a multicentre retrospective series of men with rectal cancer threatening or affecting the prostatic plane, partial prostatectomy after preoperative chemoradiotherapy resulted in a free anterior circumferential resection margin in all cases. Among patients who had preoperative chemoradiotherapy followed by prostatic resection, the CRM-positive rate was 2.4%. Without preoperative chemoradiotherapy, CRM-positive rates were higher: 25.0% with a threatened anterior margin and 41.7% with an affected margin. With preoperative radiotherapy these rates were 7.1% and 20.7%. The margin results came with morbidity: intra-operative urethral damage occurred in 36.4% of patients who underwent partial prostatectomy, and a postoperative urinary fistula developed in 18.2%.

question: Preparing patients at high risk of falls for discharge home after rehabilitation: Do we meet the guidelines?
answer: A retrospective audit of 50 high-falls-risk patients discharged home from inpatient rehabilitation found guideline-concordant preparation was incomplete: discharge documentation correctly identified falls risk for only nine of the 50 people. Risk factor assessment was limited: patients had a median of 8 of 17 risk factors, and there was little evidence of assessment for osteoporosis (n=8), footwear (n=4) or visual assessment in the previous 2 years (n=1). Patients received a median of 6.5 of 16 possible falls prevention strategies; mobility (n=48), strength (n=44) and personal activities of daily living training (n=43) were the most common, and for 12 risk factors a strategy was documented in over 80% of records when the factor was present.

question: MR Diagnosis of Bone Metastases at 1.5 T and 3 T: Can STIR Imaging Be Omitted?
answer: In a prospective whole-body MRI study of 86 patients with bone metastases, T1w sequences detected significantly more metastases than STIR at both 1.5 T and 3 T (sensitivity 99.72% at 3 T and 100% at 1.5 T for T1w, versus 70.99% and 79.34% for STIR). STIR detected fewer bone metastases than T1w in 53% (38/72) of patients at 3 T and 37.5% (18/48) at 1.5 T. Qualitatively, T1w gave significantly better lesion conspicuity, lesion delineation and image quality than STIR at both field strengths, with STIR performing especially poorly at 3 T.

question: Does cup-cage reconstruction with oversized cups provide initial stability in THA for osteoporotic acetabular fractures?
answer: In a prospective radiostereometric study of 10 patients older than 70 with acetabular fractures treated by immediate THA with an oversized cup and cup-cage, median proximal migration at 1 year was 0.83 mm and sagittal rotation 1.3°, within the limits that predict later loosening in primary THA for most components. Despite osteoporotic fracture bone, the oversized cup achieved a contact surface of 11–17 cm² (15%–27% of each component) with the unfractured pelvis, and patients were mobilized without weightbearing restrictions.

question: Utility of unenhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted MRI in children with sickle cell disease -- can it differentiate bone infarcts from acute osteomyelitis?
answer: In a retrospective study of 31 children with sickle cell disease and acute bone pain, bone marrow signal intensity on unenhanced T1-weighted fat-saturated MRI did not significantly differentiate bone infarct from acute osteomyelitis (P = 0.56). None of the other imaging parameters evaluated on unenhanced MRI reliably differentiated bone infarcts from osteomyelitis in these children.

question: Are financial incentives cost-effective to support smoking cessation during pregnancy?
answer: In a cost-effectiveness analysis based on a Phase II RCT of 612 pregnant women in Glasgow, financial incentives of up to £400 had an incremental cost of £1127 per cotinine-validated quitter at 34-38 weeks, and a lifetime model gave an ICER of £482/QALY from the NHS perspective. The per-quitter cost was similar to the £1390 per quitter obtained from Stapleton & West's published ICER tables, using the trial's incremental cost (£157) and incremental 6-month quit outcome (0.14).

question: Do Wound Cultures Give Information About the Microbiology of Blood Cultures in Severe Burn Patients?
answer: In a 13-year retrospective study of 195 severe burn patients, wound cultures carried information about blood culture microbiology: the same pathogen was found in both wound and blood in 30% of all patients and in 65% of patients with bacteremia. Of 263 bacteremic episodes in 88 patients, 44% of blood isolates had previously been documented in wound cultures, and BSI frequency rose as the Ryan score increased.

question: Treatment of contralateral hydrocele in neonatal testicular torsion: Is less more?
answer: Managing a contralateral hydrocele in neonatal testicular torsion solely through a scrotal approach (opened at the time of contralateral scrotal fixation, without inguinal exploration) appeared safe and effective: none of the 22 patients with a hydrocele developed a clinical hydrocele or hernia after an average of 7.5 years of follow-up. question: Could chest wall rigidity be a factor in rapid death from illicit fentanyl abuse?
answer: Post-mortem data from 48 fentanyl deaths suggest chest wall rigidity could contribute to rapid death: no appreciable norfentanyl was detected in 42% of cases and levels were under 1 ng/ml in another 52%, which the authors interpret as a very rapid death consistent with acute chest rigidity. Some deaths involved strikingly high fentanyl concentrations (e.g., 22 and 20 ng/ml) with no norfentanyl detected, and fentanyl elevation did not track with norfentanyl levels, in line with very rapid fatal events after rapid intravenous exposure. The authors note that rapid IV fentanyl can produce chest wall rigidity, that the shift to illicit IV supply may be driving the rise in deaths, and that users may be unaware of the rising fentanyl content of illicit opioids.

question: Does Viral Co-Infection Influence the Severity of Acute Respiratory Infection in Children?
answer: In a Spanish prospective multicenter cohort of 204 children admitted with acute respiratory infection, the number of detected viruses did not correlate with any marker of severity. Bacterial superinfection, not viral co-infection, was associated with greater severity, including PICU admission, higher clinical score, respiratory support requirement and longer hospital stay. Pneumococcal vaccination was associated with lower severity. These findings were replicated in an independent UK cohort of 97 children.

question: Does the treatment of amblyopia normalise subfoveal choroidal thickness in amblyopic children?
answer: Six months of amblyopia treatment (glasses, adaptation, patching) did not normalise subfoveal choroidal thickness in anisometropic hyperopic amblyopic children: pre- vs post-treatment thickness did not differ significantly in amblyopic eyes (p = 0.428) and the amblyopic eyes remained thicker than fellow eyes after treatment (p = 0.006). Visual acuity in the amblyopic eyes improved significantly with treatment (mean 0.35 to 0.16 logMAR, p < 0.001), so the lack of choroidal change occurred despite visual improvement. At baseline, choroidal thickness was significantly greater in amblyopic eyes than in fellow eyes (p = 0.019), and fellow eyes also showed no significant change after treatment (p = 0.343).

question: Prostate bed target interfractional motion using RTOG consensus definitions and daily CT on rails : Does target motion differ between superior and inferior portions of the clinical target volume?
answer: In a CT-on-rails study of 8 postprostatectomy patients (300 fractions), no statistically significant difference in interfractional motion was found between the superior and inferior prostate bed CTV in the left-right, superoinferior, or anteroposterior direction. Mean bone-to-target motion was small and similar in both portions: INF-CTV was 0.1, 0.5 and 0.2 mm and SUP-CTV was 0.3, 0.5 and 0 mm in the LR, SI and AP directions, respectively. Variability was numerically larger for SUP-CTV in the AP direction (SD 5.0 mm vs 2.5 mm for INF-CTV), though this was not a statistically significant difference in mean motion.
